splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) in the interpretation of ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, including the Sentencing Guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to an agency's or the Sentencing Commission's interpretation of ambiguous criminal provisions when the rule of lenity would favor the defendant. This matters because it determines whether ambiguity in criminal sentencing rules is resolved in the defendant's favor or in favor of the government's interpretation.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference, so ambiguity in criminal provisions must be resolved in the defendant's favor rather than deferring to the government's interpretation.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity, allowing courts to defer to anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous criminal provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid, deferrable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or impermissibly expands the guideline's plain text. This affects thousands of federal defendants whose career-offender status depends on prior conspiracy or attempt convictions.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson and Kisor, so inchoate offenses qualify as career-offender predicates.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 cannot receive deference and conspiracy convictions do not qualify as career-offender predicates.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must satisfy all three criminal-history disqualifiers in § 3553(f)(1) to be ineligible for safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and produces dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines even if the substance involved is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies. This affects the base offense level and career-offender status of defendants with prior state convictions involving substances not on federal schedules.

positions.label: State-law controlled substance suffices
positions.summary: Holds that USSG § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under federal law, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), eliminating mandatory consecutive 25-year sentences for stacked convictions, can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits split on whether non-retroactive changes in law, particularly the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to § 924(c), can be considered (alone or combined with other factors) as extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this, but some circuits hold the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes in law cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement attempting to allow this exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can be considered
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors, and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement permitting this is valid.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) exclusively through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or whether they may also use civil rights actions such as Bivens.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoner challenges that affect the execution of a sentence but do not directly challenge its fact or duration, such as BOP decisions on prerelease custody or earned time credits under the First Step Act. The split affects the procedural vehicles available to thousands of federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges affecting duration
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's challenge effectively seeks earlier release or transfer to less restrictive custody, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy, and civil rights claims are not available.

positions.label: Civil rights actions are also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring challenges to conditions or terms of confinement through civil rights actions even when the claims implicate the duration of confinement, as habeas is not the exclusive remedy for all prison-related claims.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether, at a supervised release revocation hearing, a district court may impose a sentence to punish the defendant for the violation, or only to facilitate the defendant's transition back into the community.
splits.description: Circuits split on the permissible purposes of a revocation sentence for supervised release violations. Some circuits allow courts to expressly punish defendants for violations, while others hold that revocation sentences should focus only on deterrence, public protection, and reentry. This affects the length and rationale of sentences imposed on hundreds of defendants annually.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, in addition to other sentencing purposes.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should not be imposed to punish defendants but rather should focus on deterrence, public safety, and facilitating reentry into the community, consistent with 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in a debtor's property becomes part of the Chapter 7 bankruptcy estate when a case is converted in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether increases in property value that occur after a Chapter 13 petition is filed but before conversion to Chapter 7 belong to the bankruptcy estate or remain with the debtor. This affects homeowners and other asset holders who convert cases and find their property has appreciated during the Chapter 13 period.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), read with § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was enacted to protect good-faith converting debtors and that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation remains with the debtor, consistent with the statute's structure and legislative history.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may adopt or change assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations across thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select or adjust actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be locked in by year-end.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during periods of absconding, so the clock does not run while the supervisee is a fugitive, preserving the court's authority to revoke supervised release.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release during absconding, and courts lack authority to extend the supervision period beyond what is specified in the judgment through a judge-made doctrine.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether the gatekeeping provision of § 2244(b)(1), which categorically bars claims previously presented in a prior habeas application, applies to federal prisoners bringing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter bar than § 2255(h) alone would impose. This affects the ability of federal prisoners to bring successive collateral attacks on their convictions.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to election administration rules like ballot receipt deadlines. The resolution determines whether such challenges can be heard before an election or must wait until after, which has practical implications for voting procedures nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office suffers a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state law allegedly dilutes or alters the weight of lawful votes through extended ballot-counting rules.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's alleged competitive injury from a ballot-counting deadline is too speculative or generalized to confer Article III standing for a pre-election challenge.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil timeline (30 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)) or the criminal timeline (14 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though arising in a criminal case, is a civil matter for purposes of the appellate filing deadline. The distinction matters because the civil deadline is 30 days while the criminal deadline is only 14 days, potentially barring otherwise timely appeals.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Rule 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal proceeding, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Rule 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' but this approach may conflict with other circuits' narrower applications of the collateral order doctrine to sealing orders. The issue affects litigants seeking to protect sensitive medical information during ongoing litigation.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that warrants immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, because delayed review risks irreparable disclosure.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as the right to seal can be adequately vindicated through other means such as protective orders or post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: Circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business and hospitality contexts. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, suggesting a circuit split on liability standards, available remedies, and the scope of protections for customers in service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for discrimination claims in hospitality or business establishments, potentially allowing claims based on a wider range of conduct.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring a more specific showing of discriminatory conduct before liability attaches in hospitality or business settings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
